title: Remembrance is framework-native, not OpenClaw-specific
summary: Remembrance is a standalone memory system designed for the new Go+Python framework. OpenClaw compatibility is an adapter, not the core design.
content: Remembrance is framework-native, built from scratch for the event-driven agentic framework. It is not an OpenClaw plugin. OpenClaw compatibility can be added later as an adapter layer. The core memory system must not depend on any external platform.

title: Go owns runtime, Python owns memory intelligence
summary: Go core handles orchestration, events, permissions, and agent lifecycle. Python Remembrance handles memory retrieval, vector indexing, context building, and scoring.
content: The language split is clear: Go owns the framework runtime (event manager, agent lifecycle, task execution, tool permissions, model routing). Python owns memory intelligence (embedding generation, vector search, hybrid ranking, context pack generation, ingestion rules). The Go framework calls Remembrance via HTTP before agent execution and receives structured context packs.

title: LanceDB is V1 vector store
summary: V1 uses LanceDB as the local embedded vector DB and SQLite for metadata/audit logs. No separate vector server needed.
content: LanceDB is chosen for V1 because it's local, embedded, Python-native, and requires no separate server. It supports vector search with metadata filtering. SQLite handles metadata, audit logs, and structured queries. LanceDB should not replace SQLite for structured data in V1. Migration to Qdrant or other vector DBs is a V2+ concern.

title: Ollama nomic-embed-text is V1 embedding provider
summary: V1 uses nomic-embed-text via Ollama for embeddings. The embedding provider is pluggable for future options.
content: nomic-embed-text (768 dimensions) is the V1 embedding model, served via Ollama's local API. The provider is pluggable: future options include bge-small-en-v1.5, nomic-embed-text-v2-moe, OpenAI embeddings, local sentence-transformers, and company-hosted services. If Ollama is unavailable, fail gracefully with a clear error — do not silently fall back to fake embeddings.

title: Context Builder is the core product
summary: The build_context function is the most important path in Remembrance. If time is limited, make this path excellent before adding secondary features.
content: The core question Remembrance answers: What context should this agent receive before doing this task? The build_context(task, project, agent) -> context_pack function is the golden path. Context packs must be short, useful, and actionable. They should include source memory IDs, prefer project memory over user memory, and summarize aggressively. Never dump raw memory objects into prompts.

title: V1 should not auto-ingest all conversations
summary: V1 only ingests manually marked important content or explicit ingest requests. Auto-ingestion of all agent responses is a V2+ feature.
content: Do not auto-ingest all conversations in V1. Only ingest memories when explicitly requested or when a candidate is manually marked as important. The event flow is: task.started → context.requested → context.built → agent.response → if marked important → memory.candidate.created → ingest. Auto-ingesting everything leads to noise and irrelevant context.

title: User memory and project memory are separate
summary: Project memory is default. User memory is only injected when relevant and explicitly requested. Clean separation between the two.
content: Every memory is scoped as project, user, framework, or agent. V1 primarily uses project and user scopes. Project memory is default and always available. User memory should only be injected when explicitly requested (include_user_memory=true) and when relevant to the current task. Cross-project search should be penalized by default.

title: Hybrid search beats pure vector search
summary: Use hybrid ranking: vector_similarity * 0.65 + keyword * 0.15 + importance * 0.10 + project_match * 0.05 + recency * 0.05
content: Do not rely on pure vector search. The hybrid ranking formula is: final_score = vector_similarity * 0.65 + keyword_score * 0.15 + importance_score * 0.10 + project_match * 0.05 + recency_score * 0.05. V1 can use simple keyword overlap for keyword_score. Project mismatch should heavily penalize results unless cross-project search is explicitly enabled.

title: OpenClaw should be an adapter, not the core design
summary: Remembrance core must not depend on OpenClaw. OpenClaw compatibility is added through an adapter layer later.
content: The design must not depend on OpenClaw. OpenClaw compatibility can be added as an adapter that translates between OpenClaw's memory format and Remembrance's schema. The adapter pattern keeps Remembrance portable and framework-agnostic.

title: No raw SQL or schema mutation through APIs
summary: Remembrance APIs must never expose raw SQL or allow schema changes. All access goes through validated Pydantic models.
content: Security rules for V1: No raw SQL exposed to agents. No schema changes from Remembrance APIs. No hard deletes (use status='deleted' instead). No shell execution from memory content. All writes must be logged to audit_log. All context packs must log selected memory IDs. Memory content is untrusted input. Project path ingestion must be allowlisted. API binds to localhost by default.

title: Context packs should include source memory IDs
summary: Every context pack output must include the memory IDs that were selected, enabling traceability and debugging.
content: Context packs must always include source memory IDs in both markdown and JSON output formats. This enables traceability: an agent or developer can look up exactly which memories were selected and why. The JSON format includes full memory metadata; the markdown format includes a Source Memories section with ID-title pairs.

title: V1 proves whether semantic context improves agent output
summary: V1 is a proof of concept. The success metric is: does semantic memory retrieval measurably improve agent behavior?
content: The primary question V1 must answer is whether semantic context injection improves agent output quality. If build_context returns relevant, concise context that measurably helps agents perform better, V1 succeeds. If not, we need to rethink the approach. V1 should not overbuild — focus on the golden path (ingest → search → build_context) and make it excellent.

title: Event-driven integration with Go framework
summary: Remembrance subscribes to framework events and responds with context packs. The Go framework calls Remembrance before agent execution.
content: The integration flow is: task.started → Go context middleware emits agent.context.requested → Remembrance builds context pack → Go injects context into agent prompt → agent.response.completed → Go emits memory.candidate.created only if manually marked important → Remembrance ingests. Remembrance should subscribe to prizm.memory.> and prizm.agent.context.requested events in the full Prizm integration.

title: Local HTTP API for V1, events for V2
summary: V1 exposes local HTTP endpoints (FastAPI). V2 adds event-driven integration with the Go framework's native event manager.
content: V1 uses FastAPI endpoints for all operations: POST /v1/memory/ingest, POST /v1/memory/search, POST /v1/context/build. The Go framework calls these via HTTP client. V2 will add event subscription (Remembrance subscribes to prizm.agent.context.requested events) and WebSocket streaming for real-time context updates. The HTTP API is the stable contract; events are additive.

title: No hard deletes in V1
summary: V1 uses soft deletes (status='deleted') instead of hard deletes. Memories are append-only for auditability.
content: V1 does not support hard deletes. When a memory needs to be removed, its status is set to 'deleted' and it is excluded from search results and context packs. This preserves the audit trail and enables future event-sourcing patterns. Hard deletes may be added in V2+ with explicit admin authorization.
